categories[1].label: … die Frauen (-innen)
help.intro: German builds words the way it builds numbers: by gluing pieces together. The two pieces to start with are the ending -in, which turns a male person-word into the female one (der Lehrer → die Lehrerin, der Student → die Studentin), and the compound noun, which fuses two nouns into one — die Schokolade + der Kuchen = der Schokoladenkuchen, das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür. Both let you understand far more than you have learnt: once you know Kuchen, you know Apfelkuchen, Käsekuchen and Geburtstagskuchen. Two rules cover nearly everything: -in is always die, with plural -innen and sometimes an umlaut (Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin); and a compound takes the gender of its last part. The umlaut in Ärztin and Köchin is checked strictly (type ae/oe if you have no umlaut keys).
help.tips[0].title: -in makes it female, -innen makes them plural
help.tips[0].text: Lehrer → Lehrerin → Lehrerinnen. Always die. Some add an umlaut: Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin, Franzose → Französin. -e words drop the e: Kollege → Kollegin, Pole → Polin.
help.tips[0].check.q: Mein Vater ist Koch und meine Mutter ist auch ____.
help.tips[0].check.why: -in makes the female form, and Koch adds an umlaut on the way: der Koch → die Köchin.
help.tips[1].title: Compounds: the last word rules
help.tips[1].text: die Schokolade + der Kuchen = der Schokoladenkuchen (der, because Kuchen is der). das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür. The first word describes; the last word says what it is and gives the gender.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: apple cake (der Kuchen), fish soup (die Suppe), children's room (das Zimmer)
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: house + door = front door (die, from Tür)
help.tips[1].trap: English 'apple cake' is two words with no gender; German fuses them and the gender comes from cake, not apple.
help.tips[1].check.q: ____ Gartentür ist offen. (der Garten + die Tür)
help.tips[1].check.why: The last part gives the gender: Tür is die, so it is die Gartentür, even though Garten is der.
help.tips[1].visual.caption: The last piece gives the article and the main meaning.
help.tips[2].title: The little joint: -s-, -n-, -e-
help.tips[2].text: Some compounds add a linking letter: Geburtstag + Kuchen = Geburtstagskuchen (-s-), Schokolade + Kuchen = Schokoladenkuchen (-n-). You will absorb these by reading; nobody learns them as rules.
help.tips[2].check.why: Geburtstag always takes the little -s- joint when it glues onto another word, just like Geburtstagskuchen.
help.tips[3].title: Read compounds from the back
help.tips[3].text: Kinderzimmer: Zimmer (room) … for Kinder (children). Haustür: Tür (door) … of the Haus. Start at the end and the word explains itself.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: living room, bedroom, bathroom — all Zimmer, all das
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: front door: a door … of the house
help.tips[3].check.q: Read it from the back: what is ein Kinderbuch?
help.tips[3].check.why: The last part says what it is — Buch, a book — and the first part says what kind: for Kinder.
help.remember[0]: -in = she, -innen = they (all women), and both are die.
help.remember[1]: In a compound, the last word is the boss: it gives the meaning and the gender.
help.context.en: Lots of women work at my company: my boss, two colleagues from Italy and a journalist. In the canteen today there's fish soup and apple cake. The apple cake is from the cook – delicious!
help.mistakes[0].why: Short vowels a/o often take an umlaut in the -in form.
help.mistakes[2].why: The compound takes the gender of its last part, der Kuchen.
help.hook: German glues words together like building blocks — learn the pieces and Apfelkuchen, Haustür and Lehrerin explain themselves.
sentences[0].english: Mr Kern is a teacher. Mrs Kern is a teacher too.
sentences[0].why: -in turns a male job word female: der Lehrer → die Lehrerin.
sentences[1].english: Paul is a student and Maria is a student.
sentences[1].why: Add -in for the woman: der Student → die Studentin.
sentences[2].english: Tom is my friend and Anna is my friend.
sentences[2].why: der Freund + -in = die Freundin — the -in makes it female.
sentences[3].english: Mr Wolf is a doctor. His wife is a doctor too.
sentences[3].why: -in, and the vowel often takes an umlaut: der Arzt → die Ärztin.
sentences[4].english: A waiter and a waitress work in the café.
sentences[4].why: der Kellner + -in = die Kellnerin — the waitress.
sentences[5].english: Max is a pupil and Lena is a pupil.
sentences[6].english: In the supermarket Anna asks a shop assistant.
sentences[6].why: der Verkäufer + -in = die Verkäuferin — the shop assistant.
sentences[7].english: Mr Berg is a cook. Mrs Berg is a cook too.
sentences[7].why: -in plus umlaut: der Koch → die Köchin.
sentences[8].english: Mrs Klein lives next to me. She is my neighbour.
sentences[8].why: der Nachbar + -in = die Nachbarin — no umlaut here.
sentences[9].english: Anna works with me. She is my colleague.
sentences[9].why: An -e man-word drops the -e before -in: der Kollege → die Kollegin.
sentences[10].english: Sabine writes for the newspaper. She is a journalist.
sentences[11].english: John is American and Mary is American.
sentences[11].why: Nationalities work the same way: der Amerikaner → die Amerikanerin.
sentences[12].english: Many female teachers work at the school.
sentences[12].why: The plural of an -in word doubles the n: Lehrerin → Lehrerinnen.
sentences[13].english: Many female students live in Cologne.
sentences[14].why: Freundin + -nen = Freundinnen — every -in plural ends in -innen.
sentences[15].english: My two female colleagues come from Italy.
sentences[15].why: Kollegin → Kolleginnen: the -in plural always doubles the n.
sentences[16].english: Many female doctors work in the hospital.
sentences[16].why: Ärztin → Ärztinnen — umlaut from the feminine, -innen for the plural.
sentences[17].english: The female shop assistants in the supermarket are nice.
sentences[17].why: Verkäuferin → Verkäuferinnen: -in doubles its n in the plural.
sentences[18].why: In a compound the last word rules: a Kuchen of Schokolade is der Schokoladenkuchen — Schokolade links with -n.
sentences[19].why: The last word decides the article: die Tür makes it die Haustür, whatever Haus is.
sentences[20].why: Apfel + Kuchen join directly, nothing in between: der Apfelkuchen.
sentences[21].why: The last word rules: das Zimmer → das Kinderzimmer, the room for the children.
sentences[22].why: die Suppe is last, so the soup wins: die Fischsuppe.
sentences[23].why: Geburtstag links with an -s: der Geburtstagskuchen — the s glues many compounds.
sentences[24].english: Two nice female neighbours live in the building.
sentences[24].why: Nachbarin → Nachbarinnen — the -in plural doubles the n.
sentences[25].english: Two female cooks are cooking in the restaurant today.
sentences[25].why: Köchin → Köchinnen: umlaut from the feminine, -innen for the plural.
sentences[26].why: das Ende is last and rules the article; Woche links with -n: das Wochenende.
sentences[27].why: der Platz is last, so der Arbeitsplatz — Arbeit takes the linking -s.
sentences[28].why: das Futter rules the article; Hund links with -e: das Hundefutter.
